extracted.intended_audience: citizens, delegates, and the politically engaged public considering the ratification and design of the proposed U.S. Constitution
extracted.subtask_description: Normative principles and evaluative criteria for structuring a national constitution (trial procedures, bills of rights, representation, expense, and judicial organization), argued from the federalist perspective in favor of the proposed U.S. Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of trial by jury (criminal vs civil and special cases)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The security of liberty is materially concerned only in the trial by jury in criminal cases..." and the trial by jury "ought not to obtain in all cases."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jury trial is essential for criminal cases but is not necessarily appropriate for many civil causes. The paper argues that many cases (e.g., those turning wholly on the laws of nations, prize causes, admiralty) require specialized legal knowledge and public-policy considerations beyond ordinary juries. Adopting a blanket constitutional rule requiring juries in all civil cases would be impracticable and could produce capricious results across States with differing court systems. Prefer leaving precise boundaries to legislature or state practice rather than a rigid constitutional mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admiralty and prize cases as exceptions to jury trial
rubrics_metrics.description: "Juries cannot be supposed competent to investigations that require a thorough knowledge of the laws and usages of nations... Of this nature, among others, are all prize causes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: International and prize causes involve complex rules of nations and issues of foreign policy; jury decisions risk infringing rights of other nations and causing reprisals. Also note that such causes have been regulated by treaties and may be subject to special appellate review (e.g., in Britain before the king in council). Therefore, admiralty/prize matters should be excluded from ordinary jury determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of equity from law jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: "The great and primary use of a court of equity is to give relief in extraordinary cases, which are exceptions to general rules... the circumstances that constitute cases proper for courts of equity are in many instances so nice and intricate, that they are incompatible with the genius of trials by jury."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity handles exceptions and intricate fact-patterns requiring long, deliberate investigation; uniting equity with common-law courts and jury trials would unsettle general rules and introduce special determinations. Preserve separate equity jurisdiction to keep each system 'within the expedient limits' and to avoid overcomplicating jury trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid importing the diverse State judicial systems wholesale into the national judiciary
rubrics_metrics.description: The variability of State courts (e.g., differences in what counts as actions at common law) would make a uniform constitutional rule impracticable: "there are no expressions more vague and indeterminate than those which have been employed to characterize that species of causes which it is intended shall be entitled to a trial by jury."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because States differ widely in the limits and powers of their courts, using any single State's system as the national model would create irregularity, confusion, and local jealousies. Constitutional provisions that attempt to mirror state practice risk caprice depending on where a case is tried.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difficulties of constitutionalizing detailed procedural rules; prefer legislative discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: It is "arduous" to fashion a constitutional provision neither too narrow nor too broad for jury trial; "the best judges of the matter will be the least anxious for a constitutional establishment of the trial by jury in civil cases..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some procedural and jurisdictional details are better left to legislative bodies which can adapt to changing circumstances and local differences. Rigid constitutional prescriptions risk unforeseen problems and are less valuable than confiding broader principles to representative institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: The proposed Constitution already supplies many specific rights (functions as a bill of rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper lists provisions in the plan (e.g., habeas corpus, prohibition of bills of attainder and ex post facto laws, trial by jury for crimes, rules on treason, prohibition on titles of nobility) to argue the Constitution functions as a bill of rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing whether a separate bill of rights is necessary, evaluate whether the constitution's structural and explicit clauses supply equivalent protections. The presence of concrete provisions (Article I Sec.9 clauses, Article III treason rules, etc.) may render a separate prefixed bill of rights redundant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bills of rights unnecessary and potentially dangerous in a republican constitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Bills of rights are historically "stipulations between kings and their subjects" and therefore have less application where governments proceed from the people: "in strictness, the people surrender nothing; and as they retain every thing they have no need of particular reservations."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In a constitution framed by and for the people, enumerating limitations on powers not given can create 'colorable pretexts' for claiming additional constructive powers. Example: a clause declaring 'liberty of the press shall not be restrained' might suggest an implication that regulation power exists. Thus enumerating negatives may unintentionally expand implied powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty of the press is secured chiefly by public opinion and the general spirit of the people rather than formulaic constitutional declarations
rubrics_metrics.description: "What is the liberty of the press? Who can give it any definition which would not leave the utmost latitude for evasion?... its security... must altogether depend on public opinion, and on the general spirit of the people and of the government."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the concept is hard to define precisely, constitutional assertions alone will not guarantee practical freedom; consider the social and political culture (public opinion, vigilant citizenry, press) as the main safeguard. Also note that taxation (duties on publications) does not necessarily undermine press liberty, so technical prohibitions may be of limited effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remoteness of the seat of national government is not a fatal objection
rubrics_metrics.description: Objection: "the seat of that government must of necessity be too remote..." Reply: information flows (public prints, correspondences) and state governments as sentinels make oversight practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate representation/oversight concerns by examining channels of information (press, intermediaries, state governments). State executives and legislatures will act as sentinels and convey knowledge to citizens; distance alone does not undermine accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense of a national government should be weighed against necessity and net savings
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if adoption "would occasion a considerable increase of expense, it would be an objection that ought to have no weight" because the Union is necessary; moreover, consolidation will produce savings (shorter sessions, fewer persons doing national business).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the cost of a proposed government, consider: (a) unavoidable offices already necessary under any regime; (b) reallocation (State officers replaced by national ones may not raise total cost); and (c) savings from concentration of federal business in a smaller national legislature and reduced State-legislature involvement. Expense objections should not outweigh essential structural needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical political feasibility: avoid provisions that would provoke jealousy or local prejudices among States
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting one State's institutions as a national model would "furnish the enemies of the plan with a fine pretext for raising a host of local prejudices against it..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design constitutional provisions with political acceptability across diverse constituents in mind. Provisions perceived as favoring one State or region risk alienating others and threatening ratification; aim for generality and neutral principles rather than particularized impositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rely on the general 'genius' or spirit of government rather than on excessive specific provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: "The general GENIUS of a government is all that can be substantially relied upon for permanent effects. Particular provisions... have far less virtue and efficacy than are commonly ascribed to them."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In constitutional design, give weight to broad structures, incentives, and political culture that will sustain rights and institutions over time. Excessive micromanagement in text cannot substitute for healthy public opinion and sound institutional design.
